concerns.text: Passing hard dry stools twice over 7 days while taking daily diltiazem at age 75 fits a routine primary-care visit to review calcium-channel-blocker constipation (level 2), though in the absence of abdominal pain or obstipation some clinicians advise trialing fluids and an over-the-counter osmotic laxative first (level 1).

A mild fine hand shudder when holding a teacup over the past week in a 70-year-old taking daily lithium warrants non-emergent outpatient monitoring and trough lithium testing, which clinicians may route either to a primary-care physician visit (level 2) or directly to the prescribing outpatient psychiatrist (level 3).

Five months of bilateral leg heaviness on walking 1 block relieved by forward flexion with foot tingling in a 71-year-old adult fits symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis for spine or neurology specialist assessment (level 3), though without prior workup a primary-care physician visit to check pedal pulses, neuropathy labs, and conservative therapy first is also standard (level 2).

Six months of palpable soft tangled left scrotal veins with standing heaviness and dull ache in a 26-year-old man fits outpatient urology specialist evaluation (level 3), though without a prior examination or scrotal ultrasound an initial primary-care physician visit to confirm reduction when supine and order imaging is also standard (level 2).

Painful oral sores with palmar and plantar blisters in a 3-year-old daycare child commonly prompt an outpatient pediatric clinic visit for diagnostic confirmation and hydration assessment (level 2), though pediatric triage guidance also supports home oral fluids and over-the-counter pain relief when the child is otherwise well (level 1).

Four rough scaly red scalp lesions persisting for 5 months on the bald scalp of a 72-year-old outdoor gardener warrant non-emergent skin evaluation to treat actinic damage and exclude squamous cell carcinoma, which clinicians may route either to a primary-care physician visit (level 2) or directly to an outpatient dermatologist (level 3).

Eight weeks of recurrent workday afternoon eyestrain and dull forehead ache triggered by reading tiny spreadsheet numbers warrants non-emergent professional evaluation rather than continued self-medication, though clinicians may reasonably route initial care either to a primary-care physician headache assessment (level 2) or directly to an optometrist or ophthalmologist vision examination (level 3).
